It seems reasonable to assume that most of the construction force would be highly specialized and would move on when the plant was finished, but some would remain as a part of the operational force. It also seems reasonable to assume that many of these employees would commute from towns on the Yellowstone River, including Hysham and Billings, as well as from areas as far south as Sheridan, Wyoming.
Even if half of the construction employees commuted from outside the area, impacts of the sudden large temporary population increase of around 6,000 people during construction, would seriously overload the study area's planning and service facilities for a period of at least five years. This overloading would happen no matter what amount and kind of planning and resources were made available and utilized.
It would be impossible to adequately meet the peak load, and attention would best be directed toward the challenges of the period when total employment associated with coal development would stabilize at permanent employment and population increases of around 1200 employees, and 1000-2000 persons. (Compared to a high of about 600 employees and 1000 persons for Scenario 1). This in itself would be a tremendous challenge, particularly if there is going to be significant Crow coal development in addition to that planned by Westmoreland Resources at the Sarpy Creek mines. Concentration on these ultimate potential impacts would require planning ahead to about the year when employment stabilizes for the duration of mining (1986 in the scenario).
